tagline.text: A Pangasinan town at land's end, where a lighthouse, caves, and emerald falls all sit close together

items.credit: Elmer B. Domingo / CC BY-SA 4.0 / Wikimedia Commons

children.text: A seaside town at the northwestern tip of Pangasinan province, where cream-colored Patar Beach, the century-old Cape Bolinao Lighthouse, an underground cave pool, and emerald waterfalls all sit close together. It pairs well with Hundred Islands for a west-coast trip through northern Luzon.

Bolinao is the northernmost coastal town in Pangasinan province, made up of a peninsula that forms the western edge of Lingayen Gulf along with Santiago Island and several other islands. It's a long way from Manila, about
6–7 hours
by bus, but its beaches, caves, waterfalls, lighthouse, and old church all sit within a day's reach by tricycle, so even a short trip can feel full.
Bolinao was a hub of maritime trade even before the Spanish era. Excavations along the Balingasay River unearthed a skull with gold-decorated teeth dating to around the
14th–15th centuries
, now on display at the National Museum in Manila. The Spanish era brought the coral-stone St. James the Great Church, and in
, under American rule, the Cape Bolinao Lighthouse was built to guide ships crossing the South China Sea.

Most of the coast is coral-stone bedrock, so pockmarked rocks and tide pools break up the stretches of sand. The same limestone terrain has carved out caves and underground pools below ground, and emerald waterfalls in the forest. A marine sanctuary offshore is restoring giant clams, making for good snorkeling too.
It suits families who want beach relaxation alongside light adventure, travelers renting a car for a west-coast drive, and anyone who wants one more quiet day of rest after seeing Hundred Islands.

A long stretch of cream-colored sand on Bolinao's west coast, where most resorts are clustered. Sunsets over the South China Sea are beautiful, but waves can run strong on some days, so swim only where the water is calm.
Standing on Punta Piedra Hill south of Patar, this roughly
-tall lighthouse has a light that sits about
above sea level, making it one of the tallest in the Philippines. The tower itself is often closed to visitors, but the view from the hilltop is superb.
Follow the stairs down underground to swim in a clear pool beneath stalactites. Admission runs about
, and the cold water is a great way to beat the midday heat.

Smaller than Enchanted Cave but with charming stalactites and its own underground pool. It draws fewer visitors, making it a quieter place to explore, and many travelers pair both caves in a single day.
Waterfalls tumbling between limestone cliffs into emerald pools, with Falls 1 and Falls 2 the most popular. Admission runs about
per site, and Falls 2 lets you jump from low rocks for fun.

blocks.title: Giant clam snorkeling off Silaqui Island

children.text: In the protected waters off Bolinao, you can snorkel among giant clams raised by research institutions and the local community. You'll need to rent a boat and a guide together, and touching or stepping on the clams is against the rules.

An old church in Bolinao town built of stacked coral stone, notable for its trefoil-arched front entrance. Having weathered earthquakes, fires, and typhoons over the centuries through repeated restoration, it stands as a symbol of the town.
A boat tour upriver through mangroves and ferns, running about
per boat. Ride in the calm afternoon for the best chance of spotting birds.

Direct buses to Bolinao run from early morning from Victory Liner and Five Star out of Cubao and Pasay, Manila. The trip takes about
6–7 hours
, with a one-way fare of around
If you miss a direct bus, take one bound for Dagupan or Alaminos, then transfer to a Bolinao-bound bus or van at Alaminos. From Alaminos it's about
1 hour

Take the NLEX–SCTEX–TPLEX north, exit into Pangasinan, then pass through Lingayen, Labrador, and Alaminos to reach Bolinao. It takes about
5–6 hours
from Manila.
Pangasinan has no scheduled flights. Coming from Korea, Clark International Airport (CRK) is the closest, about
4 hours
away by car. You can also catch a Bolinao-bound bus from the Dau terminal near Clark.
A tricycle from the Bolinao bus stop to your accommodation on Patar Beach runs about
. A full-day charter covering the caves, waterfalls, and lighthouse runs about
for up to 4 people — agree on your stops and wait times in advance.
The
November–May
dry season is best.
December–February
brings cool breezes that make tricycle touring comfortable, though the beach can see wind and waves on some days.
March–May
has the calmest seas and clearest water, best for swimming and snorkeling, with midday temperatures climbing to
. Resorts fill up early during Holy Week and summer break, so book ahead.
June–October

is the rainy season, shaped by the southwest monsoon and typhoons, and Bolinao, on Luzon's west coast, sees heavy rain and high waves. The waterfalls can swell and turn muddy, and boat tours are often canceled. Plan mostly around activities less affected by weather, like cave swimming, during this period.

Most accommodations cluster along Patar Beach. A beachfront resort facing the sea runs about
a night, while a simple guesthouse runs about

; resorts set on the rocky shore have great tide pools and views but may have less sand. Shops and restaurants are scarce around Patar, so pick up anything you need in town first. If you're driving, resorts along the road between town and Patar are also worth considering, and families may want to rent a villa-style stay with a kitchen, where you can cook seafood bought at the market yourself.

Bolinao's seafood is cheap and fresh. At resort or town restaurants, choose your own shrimp, squid, crab, or fish and have it grilled or simmered into sour sinigang. Bolinao's signature snack is binungey, sticky rice and coconut milk baked in a bamboo tube, sold around the church and market. Be sure to also try bangus (milkfish), a Pangasinan specialty, and the region's sweet mangoes.
With sights spread out, a full-day tricycle charter is the most efficient way to see them. Settle on which stops are included in the fare and the wait time at each before you set off.
Admission to the caves and waterfalls, parking, and cottage fees are all cash only. Bring plenty of small bills.
The cave stairs and rocks around the waterfalls are wet and slippery. Wear aqua shoes or trekking sandals.
Enchanted Cave gets busy on weekend afternoons. Go between
for a quieter swim.
The lighthouse tower is a coast guard facility, so access may be restricted. Plan on enjoying the hilltop view and exterior rather than going inside.
Giant clam snorkeling depends on the tide and waves, so operating hours vary. Book a day ahead through your accommodation.
If you're combining this with Hundred Islands, it's best to stay a night in Alaminos, or set out early from Bolinao, do the island hopping, and head back to Manila afterward.
There are almost no ATMs around Patar. Withdraw the cash you'll need in Bolinao town or Alaminos beforehand.
Patar Beach often has strong waves and sharp coral rock on the bottom. Most spots have no lifeguard, so if you're with children, swim only in shallow, calm areas.
Before jumping at the waterfalls, always check the water depth and rock placement, and don't swim when the water is swollen after rain.
The caves are dark with steep stairs. Hold children's and elderly visitors' hands and go down slowly.
Touching or collecting giant clams and coral in the marine sanctuary is prohibited.
During the rainy season and typhoon warnings, boat tours stop and coastal roads can flood. Check the latest weather forecast.
The sun is strong around the beach and waterfalls at midday. Apply sunscreen, and drink water often even during your tricycle tour.
